newsitem.title: USA: Risk-reversal skew seen keeping yen options edgy.
newsitem.headline: Risk-reversal skew seen keeping yen options edgy.

text.p: An extraordinary skew in pricing of yen calls over yen puts in dollar/yen options will keep the options market extremely choppy for some time, traders said Thursday.
While the skew's effect on the spot dollar/yen rate is debatable, it would certainly exacerbate any panic atmosphere that might occur if the dollar retested recent lows, they added.

"Each time the dollar goes down, dealers end up with unwanted short volatility positions and have to cover," said Masao Okada, chief options dealer at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank in New York. "Each time the dollar goes up, they become excessively long volatilities and sell options."
Risk reversals, the difference in implied volatilities for equally out-of-the-money puts and calls, have been pegged at highest levels in recent memory for weeks now.
The price skew has been caused primarily by strong end-user demand for low-delta, or out-of-the-money, yen calls for protection against a further slide in the dollar.
Such buying, often funded by yen put selling, has in turn made market-makers short in downside strike prices and long in upside strikes.
Dealers' negative gamma in the downside strikes is blown up as spot falls toward the downside strike prices, forcing short covering, and positive gamma picks up when the dollar rises.
Gamma is the rate of change in delta per move in spot, and a bigger negative gamma position is painful when spot moves around due to the larger delta-hedge spot covers required.
A U.S. bank trader agreed that recent swings in implied volatilities have been disproportionate to actual volatility.
"We haven't had such a big move in spot," he said.

Implied volatility for one-month at-the-money dollar/yen options rose as high as 12 percent on Thursday, up a full point from lows earlier in the day. The dollar, meanwhile, fluctuated largely within a 113-114 yen range.
One-month 25-delta risk reversal ended at about 2.2/2.4 on Thursday after trading as high as 2.6 and offered at 3.0. It has stayed above 2.0 for much of the past 1-1/2 months.

Buying yen calls in a risk reversal allows a delta-neutral volatility trader to reduce his negative gamma exposure on the dollar's downside without drastically changing his overall volatility position or time-decay exposure.
But payment of two percentage points in the implieds is a tough bullet to bite.

Also, risk reversals are often seen as a lagging indicator of the market's direction. Indeed, when the one-month 25-delta rose above 2.0 points the first time when the dollar fell below 112 yen on May 20, spot quickly rebounded to above 116 yen.

"We had a significant bounce the first time (the dollar tested lows)," said Alan Revercomb, options strategist at I.D.E.A. "Everyone's loading up on these downside strikes but there hasn't really been a reward for it yet"
"The thing is, it's staying (bid for yen calls)," he noted, however. "The fact that we're seeing the buying pushing further and further out the curve gives a little credibility."
Earlier in the week a U.S. investment bank was seen buying over $1 billion in notional value of six-month 30-delta risk reversal and a big one-year 10-delta was said traded Thursday.
The widening in longer-dated risk reversals might have big implications for the fortunes of many dealers.

"If you start getting a move down now, it can really hurt some P-and-Ls (profit and loss accounts) because they'd have to cover back-dated options two vols higher or three vols higher," Revercomb said. "It could really become a feeding frenzy."
Longer-dated options have higher vega, which is the rate of change in premiums per change in implied volatility.
-- Chicago Derivatives Desk ((312-408-8750))
